title: Coco Gauff escapes U.S. Open heartbreak as Mirra Andreeva wilts on Arthur Ashe Stadium
content:
NEW YORK — Coco Gauff’s dream of a third Grand Slam title, and a second at the U.S. Open, was crashing into a wall Wednesday afternoon.

For one set, Mirra Andreeva, the 19-year-old French Open champion, was as solid as she needed to be against an opponent who had one of those sets any tennis player dreads.

Gauff had no feel for the ball. She could not land a first serve with any sort of consistency. Her forehand and serve, which she has been rebuilding in earnest for the past 12 months, fell apart.

Andreeva has been trying to manage the stress of living up to her success in Paris all summer. In New York, Gauff’s struggles were the ultimate gift. Andreeva was up 4-0 after 12 minutes, and halfway home after 27, 6-2 to the good.

But then, Gauff’s difficulties crossed over the net. Andreeva tightened and started spraying balls of her own. By the middle of the second set, they were embroiled in a tentative push-pull of nerves, neither player able to step in and seize initiative on a point unless they were first forced to do so.

When they went to a tiebreak, Gauff twice faced match point. She tried the only thing that had been working half-decently on the afternoon. She charged ahead, trying to force Andreeva to make a shot to beat her. Andreeva sent a lob long on the first one; Gauff got another error on the second.

From there, Gauff rose as Andreeva unraveled. When she completed the tiebreak escape to level the match at one set all, Gauff sent a roar through her home Slam stadium and sent Andreeva reeling.

Early in the third set, Gauff chased back after a topspin lob and sent it high and deep to Andreeva, who was waiting for it inside the other baseline.

She barely swung at it. It felt like something breaking. Another error on the next point, and Andreeva hurled her racket to the ground, coming dangerously close to hitting a worker.

Her heart had been done since the tiebreak. Now her tennis soul appeared to be missing, too.

Gauff cruised from there, finishing off a 2-6, 7-6(7), 6-2 win and getting the loudest roar yet out of a stadium which, for so long that afternoon, had held its breath.

She will face Elena Rybakina in the semifinals Thursday, in a duel against the new world No. 1.

“These are the moments you dream of,” she told the crowd.

For months now, Gauff has been an increasingly bankable force in the game. The player who could hit 20-plus double faults and spray forehands every which way became a distant memory. She banged strokes, pushed forward and hit the first serves that she has always had but could not find.

For most of an hour Wednesday, that player was nowhere in sight.

In the first set, Gauff had 14 errors and three winners. She landed just 43 percent of her first serves. She had no aces and three double faults. Andreeva accepted the invitation to surge to a lead.

But early in the second set, the crowd finally had a chance to give Gauff something other than sympathy cheers. She feathered a drop shot to set up a backhand put away and Ashe came alive for the first time since she’d walked onto the court.

As Gauff finally got some footing in the match, Andreeva began to spray balls, as if the messy stuff that Gauff had brought to the court had spread across the net. Quickly, they settled into a rhythm — long baseline points that never really went anywhere, Andreeva putting the ball onto Gauff’s forehand and Gauff putting it right back.

Gauff and Andreeva have two of the best backhands in the women’s game. They also both use full Western grips on their forehands, which demands that they contact the ball just right and bend their knees sharply to meet low bounces. Sending tentative arcs back and forth is a far easier endeavour. They did plenty of that.

With neither one willing to take the initiative and neither one willing to accept the other’s gifts — double faults and forehand errors from Gauff; losses of conviction from Andreeva — they muddled their way toward a second-set tiebreak.

On a break point at 5-5, it was all Gauff could do to float a ball to the front of the court as Andreeva wound up for the putaway from short range. Andreeva swung hard and somehow dumped the ball into the net. Two points later, Andreeva coughed up another rally ball error. Gauff closed her eyes and tilted her head at the sky and let out a Serena Williams-style “Come on!”

Somehow, she was still alive, with plenty of thanks to Andreeva’s mounting errors. A game later, though, they entered the tiebreak. Someone was going to have to win the set. That person was Gauff, and after Andreeva’s flubbed overhead and flung racket, it seemed inevitable that she was going to win the decisive one too. She did.
